sections.history: Kachabeswarar is one of the old Shiva temples of Shiva Kanchi, a short walk from the Kamakshi temple. Appar mentions it in the Tevaram, which makes it a Vaippu Sthalam of the seventh century or earlier; it should not be confused with the Kachabeswarar temple at Thirukachur, which Sundarar sang. Tradition places its beginnings in Pallava times, when Kanchipuram was the dynastic capital; the Cholas are linked to its early masonry, and the present stonework is largely of the Vijayanagara and Nayak periods around the sixteenth century. The temple holds a place in Tamil letters as well: Kachiyappa Sivachariyar, remembered as the author of the Kanda Puranam, the Tamil telling of the story of Murugan, is associated with this temple and with the nearby Kumarakottam shrine.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact Dravidian complex of walled courts and shrines. Beyond the main sanctum of Kachabeswarar and the shrine of the goddess stand shrines of Thyagarajar and Sundarar, a hall of the sixty-three Nayanmars, and separate sanctums for Durga, Dattatreya and Adi Sankara. Sculpted pillars and corridors reflect the later Vijayanagara and Nayak additions, and the deity's name, drawn from the Sanskrit word for tortoise, ties the whole temple to its legend.
sections.legends: The sthala purana holds that Vishnu, in his tortoise form of Kurma, worshipped Shiva at this spot, and that the Lord took the name Kachabeswarar, Lord of the Tortoise, in remembrance. The tale joins the two great traditions of Kanchipuram, a city sacred to both Shiva and Vishnu, and shows this shrine as a place where each honours the other.
sections.festivals: The Chithirai Brahmotsavam in April or May, when the festival deities are carried in procession through the streets of Kanchipuram, and Chitra Pournami on the full moon of the same month are the main annual observances. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham and Karthigai Deepam are also kept with special worship. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: The temple sits among the busy streets near the Kamakshi temple, and a pause here is a quieter counterpoint to the larger shrines of Kanchipuram. Look for the shrine of Sundarar and the hall of the Nayanmars, and spend a moment at the sanctum of the Lord of the Tortoise. Because the great temples of the city lie close together, many pilgrims combine Kachabeswarar with Ekambareswarar, Kamakshi and the Vishnu shrines in a single day, on foot or by auto.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is on West Raja Street in the heart of Kanchipuram, a short distance from the Kamakshi temple and within walking distance of several of the city's major shrines. Kanchipuram railway station and the bus stand are a short auto ride away, and the city is linked by road to Chennai, Chengalpattu, Vellore and Arakkonam. Chennai International Airport, roughly 70 km away, is the nearest airport.
